explain:
A subscription collection was presented after three quiet years.
It was returned.
No message warned anyone it would happen.

Here is how that happens:

→ Mandate signed, collections run for a while
→ Customer pauses the service, no orders for 36 months
→ Mandate lapses silently
→ New collection presented on the lapsed mandate
→ Collection returned, service cut off

The assumption said:
"The mandate is on file. It stays valid."

So nobody tracked the last use of the mandate, and the first anyone knew it had expired was the return.

Why?

A SEPA mandate expires after 36 months with no orders related to it. Expiry triggers no message to any party. The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use.

A mandate lapses quietly. Nobody is told.

The file still held the mandate. The scheme no longer recognised it.

BA Takeaway

A mandate is a lifecycle. Track its last use or lose the collection.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate last use date, tracked
→ Expiry at 36 months, watched
→ Renewal before the next collection
→ Customer told before the collection fails

The real requirement is not "Do we hold a mandate?"

It is "What evidence proves this mandate is still alive on the collection date?"

Have you seen a collection fail on a mandate that expired in silence?
takeaway: A mandate lapses quietly. Nobody is told. Track its last use or lose the collection.

explain:
A creditor changed the collection amount for the month.
The pre-notification still showed the old amount.
The debtor disputed the collection, and it was returned.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection amount changes for the month
→ Pre-notification sent with the old amount
→ Collection presented at the new amount
→ Debtor sees a different amount from the notice
→ Debtor disputes, collection returned

The assumption said:
"Pre-notification is a formality. The file carries the real amount."

So the notice and the file drifted apart, and the debtor was asked to pay an amount nobody had told them about.

Why?

Pre-notification is the notice the creditor sends the debtor before the collection, stating the amount and the date, while collection submission is a separate step. Pre-notification is not collection submission, and if the notice is not updated, the debtor can dispute the collection. The notice and the file must stay in step.

The notice is the agreement. The file is just the execution.

The amount in the file was right. The amount in the notice was wrong, and the notice is what the debtor trusts.

BA Takeaway

When the amount changes, the notice changes first.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Amount and date in the notice
→ Amount and date in the collection file
→ Check that notice and file agree before submission
→ Dispute path when they do not agree

The real requirement is not "Is the file correct?"

It is "What evidence proves the debtor was told the amount they are about to pay?"

Have you seen a collection disputed because the notice was out of date?
takeaway: The notice is the agreement. When the amount changes, the notice changes first.

explain:
A supplier payment was promised with value today.
It arrived with value tomorrow.
The supplier charged a late fee.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment instruction complete and accepted
→ Bank collects orders until the FX cut-off
→ FX trade happens after the cut-off
→ Tenor counts from the next day, not today
→ Value date slips a day, late fee follows

The assumption said:
"The instruction is in. The value date is today."

So the team promised the value date from the instruction time, and never checked the trade time.

Why?

An FX tenor such as Today, Tomorrow or Spot counts from the day the deal is traded, provided the trade happens before the FX cut-off time. Traded today before the cut-off, a Today tenor settles today, a Tomorrow tenor settles tomorrow, and Spot settles in two days or more. A trade after the cut-off settles a day later, because once the cut-off passes the bank is already working on the next day.

The cut-off decides the value date, not the instruction.

The instruction was on time. The trade was not.

BA Takeaway

Trade before the cut-off or re-promise the value date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction time
→ FX trade time against the cut-off
→ Tenor counted from the trade day
→ Value date promised to the customer

The real requirement is not "When was the payment instructed?"

It is "What evidence proves the trade happened before the cut-off?"

Have you seen a value date slip because the trade missed the cut-off?
takeaway: The cut-off decides the value date, not the instruction. Trade before the cut-off or re-promise the date.

explain:
The MT940 statements arrived every day.
The sequence ran 12, 13, 15.
Inside the missing statement 14 sat a credit nobody noticed was gone for days.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT940 statements arrive daily
→ Field 28C checked on each statement
→ Sequence shows 12, 13, then 15
→ Statement 14 is missing, and no one asks for it
→ A credit inside statement 14 stays unreconciled for days

The assumption said:
"Reconcile the transactions. The statement numbers look after themselves."

So the team reconciled what arrived and never noticed what did not arrive.

Why?

Field 28C carries the statement number and the sequence number, pinning down exactly which statement this is and where it sits in the run. A missing statement, or one arriving out of order, shows as a gap in the 28C sequence before any transaction is examined. That makes 28C the first completeness check on every MT940 received.

A missing statement is found in the numbering, not in the money.

The transactions all reconciled. The books were still incomplete.

BA Takeaway

Check field 28C first. A gap in the sequence is a gap in the books.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Statement number in field 28C
→ Sequence number in field 28C
→ Gap chased on the day it appears
→ Transactions reconciled only on a complete run

The real requirement is not "Do the transactions reconcile?"

It is "What evidence proves every statement in the run arrived?"

takeaway: A missing statement is found in the numbering, not in the money. Check field 28C first.

explain:
A cardholder disputed a EUR 4,800 transaction.
The merchant had delivery proof.
The proof arrived a day after the scheme deadline, and the merchant bore the loss.

Here is how that happens:

→ Cardholder disputes the transaction
→ Issuer raises the chargeback with the scheme
→ Merchant gathers delivery evidence
→ Evidence arrives after the scheme deadline
→ Loss stands against the merchant

The assumption said:
"Good evidence wins. The deadline is flexible."

So the merchant built the perfect case and missed the only date that decided it.

Why?

A chargeback starts when a cardholder disputes a transaction and the issuer raises it with the scheme, and the acquirer and merchant respond with representment evidence while the scheme applies its timelines and reason codes. The financial impact moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant as the case progresses, so knowing the reason code matters: it decides what evidence is needed and who bears the loss at each stage.

The reason code is the case, not a label on it.

The evidence was perfect. It was also late, and late evidence does not exist.

BA Takeaway

Representment evidence has a deadline. Miss it and the evidence does not exist.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reason code, read first
→ Evidence the code demands, gathered fast
→ Scheme deadline, tracked as the real deadline
→ Loss owner at each stage, known in advance

The real requirement is not "Do we have good evidence?"

It is "What evidence proves our case inside the scheme deadline?"

Have you seen a winnable chargeback lost to a deadline?
takeaway: Representment evidence has a deadline. Miss it and the evidence does not exist.

explain:
A corporate submitted a pain.001 file with ten payments.
The file timed out with no confirmation.
The file was re-sent whole, and three payments were paid twice.

Here is how that happens:

→ pain.001 submitted with ten payments
→ Seven become pacs.008 to the next bank
→ Three are on-us, posted internally at once
→ Timeout, no confirmation received
→ Whole file re-sent, three on-us payments posted again

The assumption said:
"No confirmation means nothing happened. Re-send the file."

So the retry treated an unknown as a failure, and the payments that never become pacs.008 were paid a second time.

Why?

A pain.001 file promises a batch of payments, yet not every payment in the file becomes a pacs.008. When a corporate submits ten payments and only seven pacs.008 messages reach the next bank, the other three are on-us payments, where sender and beneficiary hold accounts with the same bank and the payment is handled internally. Counting only pacs.008 messages shows seven payments and suggests three are missing, while the three on-us payments were already paid. A timeout is an unknown, not a failure, and a blind retry can create a duplicate.

A timeout is an unknown, not a failure.

Seven payments could be traced by message. Three could not, and those three were paid twice.

BA Takeaway

Find the outcome first. Never retry a file blind.

Keep these controls separate:

→ File total, ten payments promised
→ pacs.008 count, seven sent onward
→ On-us count, three handled internally
→ Outcome known before any retry

The real requirement is not "How fast can we re-send?"

It is "What evidence proves which payments already settled before we send anything again?"

Have you seen a blind retry pay the same payment twice?
takeaway: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure. Find the outcome first. Never retry a file blind.

explain:
A customer paid USD 40,000 to an overseas supplier. The supplier's bank confirmed it had received funds. The supplier was never credited.

The money had landed in the beneficiary bank's own account, booked as the bank's own funds.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank with the customer instruction
→ MT202 COV sent to the funding bank to settle the funds
→ Beneficiary bank reads the cover as a plain bank-to-bank transfer
→ Cover booked as proprietary funds, MT103 left unmatched
→ Supplier unpaid, nobody can see why

The requirement said:
"An MT202 is an MT202. Book it as bank funds."

So the cover was processed without ever looking for its MT103.

Why?

An MT202 COV exists to settle one specific MT103. It carries the reference that binds the two messages together. A plain MT202 is a bank's own transfer, moving proprietary funds with no customer payment behind it. Both move money between banks, but only the COV answers to a customer instruction.

A cover without its MT103 is just money with no owner.

The beneficiary bank must recognise the cover by its reference and match it to the MT103 before booking anything. Without that link, the cover looks exactly like an ordinary bank-to-bank transfer.

BA Takeaway

A COV is not a plain MT202. The reference is what makes it a cover.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover-to-MT103 matching
→ Reference check on every MT202 COV
→ Booking of bank funds versus customer funds

The real requirement is not "How do we book an MT202?"

It is "What evidence proves this cover belongs to that MT103?"

Have you ever seen funds booked to the wrong account because a cover was read as a plain transfer?

explain:
An MT103 announced EUR 30,000. The MT202 COV that arrived to settle it carried EUR 29,965. The beneficiary bank credited nobody and raised an exception.

EUR 35 was missing, and the whole payment stopped.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent announcing EUR 30,000
→ MT202 COV arrives for EUR 29,965
→ Reference matches, amount does not
→ Sequence B of the cover does not mirror the MT103
→ Beneficiary bank holds both legs and investigates

The requirement said:
"Match on the reference. Small amount differences can be adjusted later."

So a EUR 35 gap was treated as a rounding problem instead of a broken link.

Why?

In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV must agree on amount and on the references that link them. A mismatch is not a minor data error. It is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg, and the bank must investigate before it credits the beneficiary. Sequence B of the cover must mirror the MT103 exactly wherever a field is provided, or the field must be left empty. Some banks reject a cover whose sequence B does not match the announcement, even when the amounts agree.

Two legs, one truth. If they disagree, nothing moves.

The EUR 35 was a charge taken from the cover somewhere in the chain, which is itself forbidden. The mismatch was the symptom, not the cause.

BA Takeaway

The MT103 and the cover must agree, or the payment stops.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Amount match between MT103 and cover
→ Reference match between MT103 and cover
→ Sequence B mirror check

The real requirement is not "Is the difference small enough to ignore?"

It is "What evidence proves the two legs describe the same payment?"

Have you ever seen a payment stall over a difference so small nobody wanted to own it?

explain:
A cover payment of USD 10,000 was announced. The cover that arrived was USD 9,965. The beneficiary bank refused to credit the full amount, and the USD 35 gap turned into a two-week dispute.

An intermediary had taken its charge straight out of the cover.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 announces USD 10,000
→ MT202 COV sent for USD 10,000
→ Intermediary deducts USD 35 from the cover
→ Cover arrives at USD 9,965
→ Beneficiary bank holds the payment as an exception

The requirement said:
"Intermediaries may deduct their charges from the funds they handle."

So the intermediary treated the cover like a serial payment and helped itself.

Why?

It is forbidden to take charges from an MT202 COV. The cover amount must never be lower than the amount announced in the MT103. If an intermediary needs to be paid for its part in the chain, it asks the sending bank to pay through an MT191, or debits the account directly under the agreement between the banks. A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is an exception, not a normal deduction.

Never take charges from the cover. The cover is the full amount, or it is an exception.

The MT190 and MT191 messages exist precisely for this charges leg between banks, so the payment itself is never touched.

BA Takeaway

Charges never come out of a cover payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover amount versus announced amount
→ Charges claimed through MT191
→ Intermediary agreements on direct debits

The real requirement is not "How does the intermediary get paid?"

It is "What evidence proves the cover arrived in full before we credit the beneficiary?"

Have you ever chased a shortfall that turned out to be a charge taken from the wrong place?
takeaway: Never take charges from the cover. The cover is the full amount, or it is an exception.

explain:
A customer sent EUR 8,000 to the wrong beneficiary by mistake. The recall went out the same day. The beneficiary had already spent the money.

The bank sent the recall, received a polite answer, and the funds never came back.

Here is what happened:

→ pacs.008 sent, EUR 8,000 credited to the wrong beneficiary
→ Beneficiary spends the funds the next day
→ camt.056 recall sent to the beneficiary bank
→ Beneficiary bank asks its customer whether it agrees
→ Customer refuses, no pacs.004 returns

The requirement said:
"If a payment went to the wrong person, recall it and the money comes back."

So the customer was promised a reversal that no message can deliver.

Why?

A camt.056 can still be sent to ask the beneficiary bank to return the money, but the beneficiary bank must ask its customer whether it agrees. If the funds are no longer there, the recall cannot be completed by message alone, and the customer must take action against the beneficiary. A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message: the originator bank sends camt.056 to the intermediary, which forwards it to the beneficiary bank, and the funds come back only when every bank in the chain acts.

Once the money is spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

The camt.029 answer closes the recall question by stating whether the recall was accepted or refused, but even an accepted recall does not move money. Only the pacs.004 return does that.

BA Takeaway

A recall asks. Only a return pays.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Recall request status
→ Beneficiary consent and funds availability
→ Return (pacs.004) status

The real requirement is not "When do we send the recall?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds are still there and the return is on its way?"

Have you ever had to tell a customer that a recall cannot bring spent money back?

explain:
A payment of USD 15,000 was returned because the beneficiary account did not exist. The customer waited a week, then asked where the refund was.

The return was still travelling. It had to pass through every bank that carried the payment forward.

Here is what happened:

→ pacs.008 sent for USD 15,000
→ Beneficiary bank cannot apply it, account does not exist
→ pacs.004 sent back to the intermediary
→ Intermediary forwards a new pacs.004 to the originator bank
→ Originator bank credits the customer, minus charges already deducted

The requirement said:
"When a payment is returned, credit the customer the full amount straight away."

So the customer was promised USD 15,000 while the return was still two banks away.

Why?

When a beneficiary bank returns a payment with a pacs.004, the intermediary that received it sends a new pacs.004 back to the originator bank, so the return travels the chain in reverse. The intermediary never keeps the return. It forwards it with the reference to the original payment so the originator bank can match it. A return is not a new payment. It is the original payment travelling backwards.

The charges on the return follow fields 71A and 71F, so the amount that comes back is the amount sent minus the charges already deducted. The customer is not made whole for charges the chain already took.

A return is the same payment travelling backwards, not a new payment.

BA Takeaway

A return follows the chain home, step by step.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return reference to the original payment
→ Forwarding at each bank in the chain
→ Refund amount after charges already deducted

The real requirement is not "When do we credit the customer?"

It is "What evidence proves the return has arrived and been reconciled at each step?"

Have you ever waited on a refund that was still travelling backwards through the chain?
takeaway: A return is the same payment travelling backwards, not a new payment.

explain:
A payment to Australia was returned five times over six weeks. Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A.

The code was in the message. It was in the wrong field.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent with the beneficiary bank code in field 72
→ Returned, code must be in field 57A
→ Resent with the code in field 52A
→ Returned again, code must be in field 57A
→ Resent three more times, returned every time

The requirement said:
"Put the beneficiary bank code somewhere the receiving bank can see it."

So the team moved the code around the message instead of putting it where the receiving bank reads it.

Why?

Field 57A is the field the receiving bank reads to find the account with institution. A code placed in field 72 or in field 52A can be seen by the receiving bank, but that does not satisfy the validation. The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied.

The receiving bank reads field 57A. Nowhere else counts.

A misspelt name in field 50 can return a payment for the same reason. Screening and reconciliation match on the name, and a name that does not match the account can look like a different party. Data quality failures return payments just as surely as funds failures do.

BA Takeaway

The right value in the wrong field is still the wrong field.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 57A validation before sending
→ Current BIC check for the beneficiary bank
→ Return reason read before resending

The real requirement is not "Is the code in the message?"

It is "What evidence proves the code is in field 57A and current?"

explain:
A customer sent a payment in a less common currency and was told it would arrive in two to three days. Nine days later it still had not arrived, and the customer assumed the money was lost.

The money was not lost. The bank had not bought the currency yet.

Here is what happened:

→ Payment instructed in a less common local currency
→ Bank collects orders until its cut-off time
→ Bank checks its nostro balances before buying
→ Currency bought late, payment released days after instruction
→ Customer told the standard timeline, not the real one

The requirement said:
"Tell every customer the payment takes 48 to 72 hours."

So a payment that needed a currency the bank did not hold was promised the timeline of a major currency.

Why?

A bank does not buy the currency of every payment the moment it is instructed, because it does not know in advance how much foreign currency it will need. It collects orders until a cut-off time and then decides whether to buy, sell or do nothing, based on the balance of orders and the funds already sitting in its nostro accounts. A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete.

A transfer in a major currency such as the dollar or the euro usually arrives in 48 to 72 hours, while a transfer in a less common local currency takes longer because the currency is harder to buy. A large amount can also slow a payment down, because it may need extra checks before it is released. If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem, and the sending bank should be asked to trace it, since it knows every party in the chain.

The instruction can be complete while the money waits for the bank's currency position.

BA Takeaway

The timeline follows the currency, the cut-off and the nostro balance, not the instruction date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cut-off time for the currency
→ Nostro balance before buying
→ Trace trigger when the payment passes two weeks

The real requirement is not "How long do payments usually take?"

It is "What evidence proves this currency, amount and cut-off can settle on the date we promised?"

title: EUR 10,000 to a non-euro account, euro leg done in seconds, rest waits hours
explain:
A customer sends EUR 10,000 from Europe to a non-euro account.
The euro leg finishes in seconds.
The customer expects the whole payment done.
Nothing happens for hours while the other leg is processed.

Here is how that happens:

→ Euro leg inside SEPA, completes in seconds
→ Non-euro leg outside SEPA, different rules, different timeline
→ Customer sees the euro leg finish, expects the whole payment done
→ Hours pass, nothing happens, other leg still processing

The assumption was:
"One payment, one speed, one status."

In an instant cross-border payment from Europe, the euro leg inside SEPA can complete in seconds, but the non-euro leg outside SEPA follows different rules and a different timeline.

Why?

The two legs must be explained separately, with their own coverage and responsibilities, because a single status cannot describe two different journeys. A customer who only sees the fast leg believes the payment is done, and the hours that follow look like a failure.

One status cannot describe two journeys.

Why does the customer think a half-finished payment is done?

BA Takeaway

Explain each leg separately, with its own speed, coverage and owner.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Euro leg, inside SEPA, seconds
→ Non-euro leg, outside SEPA, its own rules and timeline
→ Customer status, per leg, never one blended status
→ Responsibility, who owns each leg

Show both legs on the payment status, each with its own state and time.

The real requirement is not "Did the euro leg finish?"

It is "What evidence proves the customer saw the state of both legs?"

Have you watched a customer celebrate a leg as if it were the whole payment?
takeaway: The two legs must be explained separately, with their own coverage and responsibilities.

title: EUR 60,000 payment, app says pending, engine says processed, ledger says nothing
explain:
A customer sends EUR 60,000 abroad.
The app says pending.
The engine says processed.
The ledger has no posting.
Three systems, three truths, one customer on the phone.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment passes through several payment service providers
→ App says pending
→ Engine says processed
→ Ledger has no posting

The assumption was:
"Each system can use its own meaning of a status."

When a cross-border payment passes through several payment service providers, each one can show a different status: the app says pending, the engine says processed, and the ledger has no posting.

Why?

The customer and the contact centre cannot tell whether the money has left, arrived, or is lost. The fix is consistent status meanings, a status enquiry path and clear customer communication at every step, because a payment whose state cannot be stated cannot be managed.

Three statuses, no truth.

Why can no one tell the customer where EUR 60,000 is?

BA Takeaway

Give every status one meaning everywhere, and give the customer a way to enquire.

Keep these controls separate:

→ App status, what the customer sees
→ Engine status, what processing says
→ Ledger posting, what the money did
→ Status enquiry, the path to the true state

Map every local status to one shared meaning, and show the ledger truth beside the app status.

The real requirement is not "What does the app say?"

It is "What evidence proves the status the customer sees matches the ledger?"

Have you told a customer pending when the engine said processed?
takeaway: A payment whose state cannot be stated cannot be managed.

title: EUR 70,000 to a supplier, screen says pending, supplier says unpaid
explain:
A company sends EUR 70,000 to a supplier.
The screen says pending.
The supplier says it has not been paid.
The clerk cannot say where the money is, because the status hides every step in the middle.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment travels through a bank, a correspondent and the supplier bank
→ Customer screen shows only one status, usually Pending
→ Supplier says it has not been paid
→ Clerk cannot say where the money is

The assumption was:
"One status is enough for the customer."

A payment that travels through a bank, a correspondent and the supplier bank shows only one status on the customer screen, usually Pending, while the supplier says it has not been paid.

Why?

The clerk cannot say where the money is because the status does not reflect the intermediary steps. Customer-facing statuses must stay accurate while the underlying processing is still pending, so the customer is not left guessing.

Pending hides the journey.

Why can the clerk not say where EUR 70,000 is?

BA Takeaway

Show the intermediary steps, and keep the customer status accurate while processing is still pending.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bank leg, where the payment left
→ Correspondent leg, where it travels between banks
→ Supplier bank leg, where it lands
→ Customer status, accurate at every step, never a single flat Pending

Show each leg with its own state, so the clerk can point to the exact step.

The real requirement is not "Does the screen say pending?"

It is "What evidence proves the customer can see where the payment is, leg by leg?"

Have you told a supplier the payment is pending when you could not say where it was?
takeaway: Customer-facing statuses must stay accurate while the underlying processing is still pending.

title: One payment, two amounts: USD 100,000 in, USD 99,400 out
explain:
A customer instructs a cross-border payment of USD 100,000.

The beneficiary receives USD 99,400.

Nobody stole the difference. A rule took it.

Here is how it happens:

→ pain.001 instructs USD 100,000
→ Payment engine validates and converts to pacs.008
→ Clearing applies fees and an FX conversion at a shifted value date
→ Clearing settles USD 99,400

The assumption was:
"The instructed amount is the settled amount."

Why?

The payment engine and the clearing layer apply different rules. The engine validates the instruction, while clearing settles a different amount after fees, charges or an FX conversion at a shifted value date.

The amount gap always has a rule behind it.

BA Takeaway

Start the investigation by comparing the instructed amount in the pacs.008 against what clearing actually settled, then find which rule changed it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instructed amount in pacs.008
→ Amount clearing actually settled
→ Value date and charges applied

The real requirement is not "Why is the amount different?"

It is "What evidence proves which rule changed the amount?"

Have you chased an amount gap and found the rule hiding behind it?
takeaway: The amount gap always has a rule behind it. Compare pacs.008 against what clearing settled.

title: The payment settled, but Treasury funded from a stale screen
explain:
A payment settles correctly.

Treasury funds from the screen. The screen is stale.

The real funding need moved from USD 2 million to USD 5 million before cut-off, and nothing alerted Treasury.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment settles correctly
→ Nostro ledger feed fails
→ Treasury screen still shows USD 2 million
→ Real funding requirement moves to USD 5 million
→ Nothing alerts Treasury before cut-off

The assumption was:
"Treasury will see the funding need on screen."

Why?

The payment settled, but the Nostro ledger feed failed silently. Treasury kept making funding decisions from outdated data, which is a critical operational risk even though no payment failed.

A settled payment can still leave the bank blind.

BA Takeaway

A feed failure is a funding risk, not just a data issue. Treasury needs a live feed and an alert when the feed stops, not just a screen.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payment settlement
→ Nostro feed health
→ Treasury funding view

The real requirement is not "Did the payment settle?"

It is "What evidence proves the funding screen is live, not stale?"

Have you seen a desk make a funding decision from data that had already gone stale?
takeaway: The payment settled, but the bank was making funding decisions from outdated data.

title: One statement line, 400 entries, and one missing
explain:
A settlement batch holds 400 entries under one statement line worth EUR 850,000.

One entry is missing.

The whole group fails, and nobody can tell the customer why.

Here is how it happens:

→ Settlement happens in a batch
→ One statement line stands for 400 ledger entries
→ Entries share one batch reference
→ One entry is missing
→ The whole group fails reconciliation
→ A temporary GL entry is raised while investigating

The assumption was:
"Match each entry to the statement."

Why?

Reconciliation must collect the entries by batch reference and reconcile that group as one against the statement line, rather than matching a single entry. If one entry is missing, the whole group fails.

Reconcile the batch, not the entry.

BA Takeaway

The engine must preserve the batch reference linkage across the items. Grasp the reason the batch exists, not merely how it matches.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Batch reference linkage
→ Group reconciliation
→ Missing entry handling

The real requirement is not "Does this entry match?"

It is "What evidence proves the batch reference survives across every entry?"

Have you seen one missing entry fail a whole batch reconciliation?
takeaway: Reconcile the batch, not the entry. One missing entry breaks the whole group.

title: The optional field that stopped a EUR 120,000 cover payment
explain:
In a four-bank cover payment, Bank A sends pacs.008 to Bank B and a pacs.009 cover to intermediary Bank C.

Bank C cannot link the cover to the customer payment.

The EUR 120,000 cover sits unreconciled, because one optional field was left out.

Here is how it happens:

→ Bank A sends pacs.008 to Bank B
→ Bank A sends pacs.009 cover to Bank C
→ Bank C must link the cover using the same UETR and remittance reference
→ The pacs.009 RltdRmtInf field is left out, because it is optional
→ Bank C cannot reconcile the cover

The assumption was:
"Optional means we can leave it out."

Why?

The pacs.009 RltdRmtInf field carries the link, and although it is optional in the message, the intermediary cannot reconcile the cover without it.

Optional in the message, mandatory for the flow.

BA Takeaway

Optional or mandatory is a property of the message, not of the process. Handle the message flow and the field status as two separate things.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message field status
→ Process need for the field
→ Reconciliation link

The real requirement is not "Is the field optional?"

It is "What evidence proves the intermediary can link the cover?"

Have you seen an optional field left out, and the whole flow stall because of it?
takeaway: Optional in the message, mandatory for the flow. A field marked optional can still be required to make the payment work.

title: The settlement that looked fine, and the Rs. 18 lakh that did not reconcile
explain:
Card payments clear for the day, and customers see their payments succeed.

Behind the scenes, the ledger is Rs. 18 lakh out from the settlement position.

Nobody notices, because nobody compared the three records.

Here is how it happens:

→ Clearing completes
→ Settlement position is the net amount each bank owes or is owed
→ Ledger postings are made
→ Clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings do not agree
→ The break is not investigated

The assumption was:
"The customer payment succeeded, so settlement is fine."

Why?

After clearing, the settlement position must match the ledger postings exactly. Reconciliation compares all three records, and any break between them is investigated rather than written off.

A settlement that does not reconcile is a control failure.

BA Takeaway

A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, even if the customer-facing payment appeared to succeed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Clearing records
→ Settlement position
→ Ledger postings

The real requirement is not "Did the payments clear?"

It is "What evidence proves clearing, settlement and ledger agree?"

Have you seen a settlement break found days after the customers had already been told everything was fine?
takeaway: A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, even if the payment appeared to succeed.

title: Approved for Rs. 15 lakh, and the money never arrived
explain:
A loan is approved for Rs. 15 lakh.

The customer waits. The money never arrives.

The team checks the approval first, and finds nothing wrong. The break is somewhere else.

Here is how it happens:

→ Approval is given
→ Account validation runs
→ Disbursement instruction is sent
→ Ledger posting is recorded
→ Customer communication goes out
→ One of these stages breaks, and the customer simply sees that the money has not arrived

The assumption was:
"The approval was the problem."

Why?

A valid approval with a wrong account, a failed instruction or a missing ledger posting all look the same to the customer, who simply sees that the money has not arrived.

Check each stage in order rather than assuming the approval was the problem.

Trace the path from approval through account validation, the disbursement instruction, the ledger posting and the customer communication, because the break can sit at any of these points.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Approval
→ Account validation and instruction
→ Ledger posting and communication

The real requirement is not "Was the loan approved?"

It is "What evidence proves which stage broke?"

title: EUR 200,000 announced, but the funds had not arrived yet
explain:
An MT103 announced EUR 200,000 to the beneficiary bank.
The beneficiary called, asking where the money was.
The funds leg had not arrived yet, and the beneficiary had not been credited.

Here's how that happens:

→ → MT103 reaches the beneficiary bank first
→ → MT202 COV still in transit
→ → Beneficiary bank holds the instruction
→ → Beneficiary asks for money that has not settled

The assumption was:
"The MT103 arrived, so the money is here."
In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV travel separately.

Why?

The beneficiary bank must hold the instruction and wait for the cover, because it cannot credit the beneficiary until the funds have settled. This timing gap is a normal feature of the cover method, not an error.

MT103 first, funds later, is normal. Crediting early is the error.

What proves the funds have settled, not just been announced?

BA Takeaway

Hold the MT103 until the cover arrives. Credit only on settled funds. Use the waiting time to check that the amount and the reference on the cover match the announcement.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction received
→ Cover received
→ Amount and reference matched
→ Funds settled

The real requirement isn't "Has the MT103 arrived?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds have settled, not just been announced?"

EUR 200,000 arrived at the beneficiary bank as an MT202 COV.

Why?

When an MT202 COV reaches the beneficiary bank, the bank must recognise that its purpose is to cover a specific MT103, and the link is the reference and the fields that tie the two messages together. Without that link the cover looks like an ordinary transfer.

The reference is the bridge between the information leg and the funds leg.

What proves this cover belongs to that MT103?

Match the cover to the MT103 on reference and fields, not on amount alone. Hold the funds until the link is proven, and send the cover back for correction if the reference is missing.

→ Fields tie the two together
→ Funds matched before credit

The real requirement isn't "Has the cover arrived?"

It's "What evidence proves this cover belongs to that MT103?"

explain:
USD 100,000 was sent through two intermediary banks.

Field 71A states who bears the charges, and field 71F states the amount of each charge deducted, so the credit can be reconciled against the amount the ordering customer sent. Without those fields the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent.

Without fields 71A and 71F, the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent.

Read the final credit from fields 71A and 71F. Check field 71A for who bears the charges and every field 71F for the amount deducted, and hold the credit until the arithmetic balances.

→ Amount instructed
→ Field 71A
→ Each field 71F
→ Final credit

The real requirement isn't "Is the credit the right amount?"

It's "What evidence proves this final credit is the amount sent minus the agreed charges?"

title: EUR 130,000 cover, and the two legs disagreed by EUR 500
explain:
A EUR 130,000 cover payment arrived.
The MT103 said EUR 130,000. The MT202 COV said EUR 129,500.
The beneficiary bank would not credit a cent until someone explained the EUR 500 gap.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 announces EUR 130,000
→ MT202 COV arrives for EUR 129,500
→ Amount and reference do not agree
→ Bank investigates before crediting

The assumption was:
"A EUR 500 difference is a minor data error."
A mismatch is a break in the link between the legs.

Why?

In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV must agree on amount and on the references that link them, and a mismatch between the two creates an exception that stops settlement. The discrepancy can be a different amount, a missing reference or details that do not line up.

A mismatch is not a minor data error. It is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg.

What proves the two legs of this cover payment agree?

BA Takeaway

→ Amount on the MT202 COV

title: EUR 100,000 cover rejected even though the amounts agreed
explain:
A EUR 100,000 cover payment arrived with the amounts matching exactly.
The beneficiary bank rejected it anyway.
Sequence B of the MT202 COV did not mirror the MT103.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 and MT202 COV amounts agree
→ Sequence B of the cover differs from the MT103
→ Beneficiary bank rejects the cover
→ Funds stop even though the amounts agree

The assumption was:
"If the amounts agree, the cover will pass."
Some banks reject a cover whose sequence B does not match the announcement.

Why?

In sequence B of an MT202 COV, only the ordering and beneficiary customer information in fields 50a and 59a is mandatory, and the other fields are optional. When the bank does provide a field such as field 72 or field 59, it must match the same field in the MT103 exactly, or the field must be left empty.

A mismatch in sequence B stops the funds even when the amounts agree.

What proves sequence B of the cover mirrors the MT103?

BA Takeaway

Mirror the MT103 in sequence B: fields 50a and 59a always, and any other field provided must match the MT103 exactly or be left empty. Check the mirror before sending the cover.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Fields 50a and 59a
→ Other fields match or empty
→ Amounts agree
→ Cover accepted

The real requirement isn't "Do the amounts agree?"

It's "What evidence proves sequence B of the cover mirrors the MT103?"

takeaway: A mismatch in sequence B stops the funds even when the amounts agree.

title: USD 100,000 credit that did not match the equation
explain:
USD 100,000 was instructed.
The beneficiary bank credited an amount that did not fit the charges equation.
The operations team could not say whether the credit was right, because no one had checked the arithmetic.

Here's how that happens:

→ Field 33B states the amount instructed
→ Field 71G states receiver charges prepaid by the sender
→ Field 71F states each charge deducted
→ Field 32A must equal 33B plus 71G minus all 71F

The assumption was:
"The system works the credit out, so the arithmetic takes care of itself."
The relationship always holds, and it must be checked.

Why?

Field 32A is the amount that settles between banks, field 33B is the amount the ordering customer instructed, field 71G is the receiver's charges prepaid by the sender, and field 71F is each sender's charge deducted along the way. The relationship always holds: 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges.

32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges. If the equation does not balance, something is wrong.

What proves this credit balances under the charges equation?

BA Takeaway

Check the equation on every payment: 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges. Remember that field 71A is set by the bank that generates the MT103 and cannot be changed by later banks, which can only add a 71F when they take a charge.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 32A
→ Field 33B
→ Field 71G
→ Each field 71F
→ Field 71A set once

The real requirement isn't "Is the credit about right?"

It's "What evidence proves this credit balances under the charges equation?"
